title: prefixSet: Simplex Vertices as Prefix Finsets
content: prefixSet l k computes the first k elements of list l as a Finset, representing the k-th vertex of the Freudenthal simplex corresponding to permutation l. The Freudenthal triangulation assigns to each permutation l : List (Fin n) a simplex whose vertices are the sets {l[0]}, {l[0],l[1]}, ..., {l[0],...,l[n-1]} — precisely the prefix sets at positions 1, 2, ..., n. This Finset representation converts the adjacency question from a geometric problem (two simplices share a face) into a combinatorial one: how many k-element sets lie between two consecutive prefix sets?
mathContext: $$\text{prefixSet}(l, k) = \{l[0], l[1], \ldots, l[k-1]\}$$ defined as $(l.\text{take}\; k).\text{toFinset}$. For a permutation $l$ of $\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$, these are the vertices of the Freudenthal simplex: vertex $k$ is $\{l[i] : i < k\}$.
significance: The key data structure enabling the reduction from geometric adjacency to Finset combinatorics. All results follow from properties of List.take and List.toFinset.

title: Consecutive Prefix Sets Differ by a Singleton
content: prefixSet_succ_sdiff proves: for a nodup list l and index k < l.length, the difference prefixSet l (k+1) \ prefixSet l k is exactly the singleton {l[k]}. The proof works by set extensionality: x is in the difference iff it is in l.take(k+1) but not in l.take(k). Using List.take_succ, l.take(k+1) = l.take(k) ++ [l[k]], so x ∈ l.take(k+1) means x ∈ l.take(k) (contradicting 'not in prefixSet l k') or x = l[k]. The nodup hypothesis ensures l[k] ∉ l.take(k) (otherwise l would have a repeated element at positions < k and = k).
mathContext: $$\text{prefixSet}(l, k+1) \setminus \text{prefixSet}(l, k) = \{l[k]\}$$ since $l.\text{take}(k+1) = l.\text{take}(k) \mathbin{++} [l[k]]$ and $l[k] \notin l.\text{take}(k)$ by \texttt{l.Nodup}.
significance: The foundational property: each step of the prefix chain adds exactly one new element. This implies prefixSet_skip_sdiff_card (the 2-element gap) and is the root of the adjacency count.

title: Two-Step Gap Has Exactly 2 Elements
content: prefixSet_skip_sdiff_card proves: for a nodup list l with k < l.length and k > 0, the difference prefixSet l (k+1) \ prefixSet l (k-1) has cardinality 2. The proof uses Finset.card_sdiff (which gives card(B\ A) = card(B) - card(A) when A ⊆ B), plus the cardinality calculations: card(prefixSet l (k-1)) = k-1 and card(prefixSet l (k+1)) = k+1. Then (k+1) - (k-1) = 2 by omega. The gap {l[k-1], l[k]} has exactly these 2 elements — they are the two elements added in two consecutive steps.
mathContext: $$|\text{prefixSet}(l, k+1) \setminus \text{prefixSet}(l, k-1)| = (k+1) - (k-1) = 2$$ using \texttt{Finset.card\_sdiff} and the cardinality formulas for prefix sets.
significance: The direct input to intermediate_sets_card_eq_two. Together with the chain condition (prefixSet l (k-1) ⊆ prefixSet l (k+1)), this identifies the 2-element 'gap' that gives exactly 2 intermediate sets.

title: Key Counting Lemma: Exactly 2 Intermediate Sets When Gap = 2
content: intermediate_sets_card_eq_two is the combinatorial core: if A ⊆ B and |B \ A| = 2, then there are exactly 2 sets S satisfying A ⊆ S ⊆ B and |S| = |A| + 1. The proof proceeds: (1) Use Finset.card_eq_two to extract a, b with B \ A = {a, b}. (2) Show the filter equals {A ∪ {a}, A ∪ {b}} via convert_to and Finset.card_pair. (3) For any S satisfying the conditions, extract the unique element e = S \ A (which is a singleton since |S \ A| = 1), show e ∈ B \ A = {a,b}, and reconstruct S = A ∪ {e}.
mathContext: $$|B \setminus A| = 2 \implies |\{S \mid A \subseteq S \subseteq B,\; |S| = |A|+1\}| = 2$$ The two sets are $A \cup \{a\}$ and $A \cup \{b\}$ where $B \setminus A = \{a, b\}$.
significance: The abstract combinatorial lemma that makes the adjacency theorem a one-liner: once we have the 2-element gap, the adjacency count is exactly 2. The proof is the longest in the file (~55 lines) but is purely Finset manipulation.

title: Freudenthal Adjacency Theorem: Exactly 2 Simplices per Interior Facet
content: freudenthal_adjacency_theorem is the main result: for a Freudenthal simplex l (nodup list of length n) and interior position 0 < k < n, the filter counting k-element sets S between prefixSet l (k-1) and prefixSet l (k+1) has cardinality exactly 2. The proof is elegant: after rewriting k = (prefixSet l (k-1)).card + 1 (since card = k-1 for interior positions), it reduces to intermediate_sets_card_eq_two by providing the 2-element gap from prefixSet_skip_sdiff_card. The full geometric argument — that these 2 sets are the vertex sets (at level k) of exactly 2 adjacent simplices — is contained in the freudenthal_two_intermediate_sets corollary.
mathContext: $$\left|\left\{S \mid \text{prefixSet}(l,k-1) \subseteq S \subseteq \text{prefixSet}(l,k+1),\; |S| = k\right\}\right| = 2$$ proved by: $|\text{prefixSet}(l,k+1) \setminus \text{prefixSet}(l,k-1)| = 2$ (prefixSet\_skip\_sdiff\_card) $\implies$ exactly 2 intermediate sets (intermediate\_sets\_card\_eq\_two).
significance: The culminating theorem. The Freudenthal adjacency theorem is a fundamental result in triangulation theory, underlying applications to Sperner's lemma (coloring argument needs exactly 2 simplices per interior edge) and Brouwer's fixed point theorem.

title: Existence Corollary: The Two Adjacent Simplices Exist Explicitly
content: freudenthal_two_intermediate_sets is the existential corollary: there exist two distinct Finsets S₁ ≠ S₂, both lying between prefixSet l (k-1) and prefixSet l (k+1) with cardinality k. The proof applies Finset.card_eq_two to the count from freudenthal_adjacency_theorem to extract the two elements, then retrieves their membership properties from the filter. This gives the user two explicit Finsets — the vertex sets (at level k) of the two Freudenthal simplices sharing the interior facet — without requiring them to work through the counting argument.
mathContext: $$\exists S_1 \neq S_2,\; \text{prefixSet}(l,k-1) \subseteq S_i \subseteq \text{prefixSet}(l,k+1) \text{ and } |S_i| = k$$ for $i = 1, 2$, extracted from \texttt{freudenthal\_adjacency\_theorem} via \texttt{Finset.card\_eq\_two}.
significance: The user-facing version of the adjacency theorem: provides two distinct explicit witness sets. For applications to Sperner's lemma, one needs to exhibit the two adjacent simplices, not just count them.
